review:
With the abandonment of the game, let's have a closer look at what might have been the reasons behind Dawn of War 3's underperformance.

Let's open this review with the following statement: I have a total of 560 hours played across DoW2 and an undeterminant amount of DoW1 from the pre-steam era. So why have I not even reached a full day in Doge of Water Drei? Contrary to some statements, it might not be the MOBA aspects everyone harps about.

A big part of it comes to gameplay style. DoW1 and 2 were very different beasts. DoW 1 had basebuilding, permanent on-the-field reinforcement for your infantry squads and relatively low impact abilities. It had a morale system, where squads that lost their morale would become useless in combat, but did gain increased movement speed to withdraw.

DoW 2 by comparison removed basebuilding, gave units higher impact abilities but in turn, reduced army size. This allowed the player to better manage their units to make use of and counter the high impact abilities. On the field reinforcements is only allowed under certain conditions and units will otherwise have to return to HQ. But there's a handy retreat button you can hit. Slam it and they run back all on their own, allowing you to continue focussing on the combat.

DoW3... tries to combine the two games. Basebuilding returns in glorious fashion from DoW1, as does the army size. DoW2's high impact abilities also sticked around. Reinforcements go by DoW2 rules, but they removed the handy retreat button. There's also no morale system or any other movement speed to help folks escape... and at this point, you might be seeing a problem. 

A larger army whilst maintaining the same fast kill potential of DoW2 means that units wipe out more easily. Not only that; the UI felt a lot more muted to me then previous installments. By the time I noticed an unit was in trouble, it was often too late. Even if I saved them, the added hassle of manually commanding them to go back to the base to reinforce, as well as replacing any units wiped out, became a chore that simply wasn't fun. In the first two games, I could make efforts to preserve my units and whilst it's still possible in DoW3, the skill to do so is placed far higher thanks to the inherent chaos of the game, thus making it unfriendly for casuals. And when I do not like the additional chores that exasperate me even when i'm winning, why would I bother reaching the level of skill where I can penetrate the veil of disarray.

Moving on to another aspect of the game. Warhammer fantasy and 40k alike have a large focus on its race variety. Simply look at the Total War: Warhammer. Despite having most major factions playable (as well as some minor ones), there are still people lamenting the absence of the Ogre Kingdoms, Daemons of Chaos and Chaos Dwarves and looking forward to TW:WH 3 for their addition. Let's look at DoW 1 and 2. Vanilla DoW 1 starred the Space Marines, Chaos, Orkz and Eldar. Vanilla DoW 2 featured almost the same lineup, with tyranids replacing evil space marines. DoW 3 brings... Space Marines, Orkz and Eldar. A mere 3 races. All their hopes was settled on the customizations option in your choice of elites and doctrines.

The problem with doctrines, besides that some are considerably stronger then others, is that they are inheritantly boring as a customization option due to most being passives. Some grant a grenade ability to one unit or some other ability, but most is a plain boring passive. As a customization option that defines your army, it's not exhilarating. Your only option for customization in DoW2 was which commander you picked, but it would change which commander you had, the abilities of your units and even added a unit to your roster! Those are impactful, visual customization options and would be preferable (if not for problems stated earlier in the review).

As for the elites, I have no inherent gameplay problem with them. My problem with them is more... flavour. The feel of the game. When you choose your "elites", unique powerful units you can deploy during the match, you can pick the usual suspects. Force Commander, Librarian, Chaplain, Warboss, Farseer and so on; traditional commander units in other words. But other options for elites are whole squads or vehicles, such as striking scorpions, kill team, terminators, venerable dreadnought and of course the posterboy mini-titans featured in trailers. The fact you could field not a single commander elite simply feels... wrong? In DoW1, you didn't  have to train a commander unit, but you did because they were powerful. In DoW 2 you started with the one commander, but even then there were sub-commanders you could train and all this feels in flavour with warhammer. It's always been about the named characters, not the faceless mobs, when it comes to theme and setting. The ability to ignore commanders in DoW 3 adds to the overall disconnection to the rest of the series.

This was my review, thank you for reading the giant wall.

EDIT: A commentator added one more interesting change DoW3 made compared to the previous two titles that in hindsight is important and might not have helped the devs balance the game; Armour and Damage Types. In the previous games, you had a smorgasboard of various types. Infantry armour, heavy infantry, vehicles and so on for armour and flamer, plasma, pierce and so on for damage. This is reduced to two types of armour; normal and heavy, and three types of damage; one to counter normal armour, one to counter heavy armour and pure true damage (a damage type that was fairly rare amongst the unit roster)

Now at first, this doesn't  necessarily seem horrible. You still have the idea of counters and as the saying goes "Sometimes less is more". At best, you may say it turned the game bland by simplefying to counter minigame to a binary choice. But there's always a limit to how far you can go. This reduction to essentionally two types of both meant that changes to a single unit will change its overall performance greatly. It won't just change their effectiveness against low tier units, but also high tier units. The different damage types and armours created layers that inhibited how far changes could reach throughout the entire unit roster of the game, allowing for more control when seeking to balance the game.

I have, admittedly, not played the game enough to say much on multiplayer balance... but even in the singleplayer campaign, unit interaction felt slightly off because of this change. Like many of the other things mentioned in this review, it's that nagging feeling that something isn't quite right and you can't put your finger on it until you start asking yourself "Why does this feel strange?" and look into the answer.

And then, after many months of not playing the game, you decide to make and edit a review of the game that's way too long because you felt a simple "It's bad" wasn't good enough.

Dawn of War 3 was supposed to combine the best elements of the previous two games, but instead it simplified or removed almost everything that made the Dawn of War series great.

The game is focused almost exclusively around elite units (heroes), while all other units are completely de-emphasised.
Interesting mechanics such as cover are removed entirely.
The economy is ruined, with resource rates being based primarily on the current game time to try to force specific game lengths.

The singleplayer campaign is uninspiring and badly written, and with the emphasis on unit-only missions and the broken economy it doesn't even feel like a strategy game.  Playing on harder difficulties just means you have to stand around for long amounts of time waiting for your units to regenerate because there's nothing else you can do.

The incredible voice acting from earlier Dawn of War games is gone, replaced by terrible and generic-sounding voiceovers.

The saddest thing is that the failure of this terrible game has most likely doomed the prospect of any future high-quality 40K real-time strategy games.

After being warned by 2 people not to buy it I did anyways... because its Relic and hey I have every other Relic game. Well unfortunately this isn't every other Relic game. The best part of it is actually the intro video.

-Campaign is HORRIBLE. Like the worst I have ever played. It's linear, uninteresting, and on Hard, frankly unplaytested. You will have no reason to ever replay it, but you have to play it on hard to get the stupid skulls. Prepare to hate yourself as you grind your way through it.
-Multi has a progression system that literally prevents you from trying other armies because everything costs skulls and has arbitrary exp gating. It doesn't fit at all with how they designed the game, you should have everything unlocked from the start. I feel like this is the biggest turn off to casual players, it has a freemium grind system paired with a premium game price. Ridiculous.
-Gameplay in multi is either 1V1 where you instantly lose due to someone with superior micro, which is fine, not my cup of tea. But there really isn't any back and forth, you will get utterly trounced. 3V3 is a goddamned turtle fest until escalation point 3 where the game explodes into a total blob fest, with the biggest blob winning. Oh and throughout all of this elites are basically gods that shred line troops, giving them almost 0 value. Unit preservation was always a big staple of Relic games, but nope thats gone. Fodder troops and OP elites, thats what you get.

Sadly the game is already dying, and its harder and harder to find matches. The player count is now well below even COH2 which is a 5 year old title. 

Wait for a sale, or just don't bother. I don't know who these devs are but frankly this is a game that was developed for a fanbase that didn't want it, by a dev team that was completely clueless. It feels like they eviscerated every part of what made their studio great and tried to copy starcraft with a DOW style paintjob.

[Update June 5th]

Okay so the game has been out a month now and here are the changes: 

Relic upped the resource requisition rate which effectively killed the entire early game. Matches now go from 0 to full blob explosion in roughly 10 minutes. Where matches used to last 30 -40 minutes, the average mach time is now sub 20. The current meta is to spam hordes of OP devastators wtih the recently super buffed space marines. With the increased req rate the value of line units has degraded to basically completely worthless, and you will just be attack moving your blob forward as you go. Lose an entire army? No big because you can rebuild it in minutes. Want strategic depth? Why would you do that when you can just build infinite amounts of artillery units to try and counter the infantry blobs. The game play is such a mess right now.

Eldar were nerfed into the ground completely, even top tier eldar player Cataclaw is complaining that the eldar are no longer viable competitively.

Match making now takes on average 10 - 20 minutes to get a game due to the fact that as of an hour ago less than 800 people were online and of those 800 people you can bet some of them were slogging there way through the unbearable campaign.

I find it difficult to comprehend some of the changes that were made and the length of time it took to make them. It honestly feels like relic listened only to the feedback of the most vocal (read as biased) top tier players and made changes, some of which are baffling. 

The player base is almost non existent outside of weekends, and the patch had almost no effect at bringing people back into the game. 

Please please do not buy this game unless you are getting it for under $20, and even if you do purchase it be prepared to wait A LONG TIME for any kind of competitive multiplayer match. I can't wait to see what the player numbers look like 2 months from now if the community lost 95% of its players in 1.

[Update July 10th]

Relic released a public apology for the state of the game a couple weeks ago and the new "annihilation mode", which to their credit is actually pretty good and caters more to the fans of DOW1 & 2. Annihilation offers both a turret doctrine and some changes to the power core maps, and an additional 1 map.

Unfortunately I don't know if this, or any future update can save the game because I tried logging in a few minutes ago and it took 20 minutes in waiting for a 3 V 3 automatch game and there were only 2 custom games available in the lobby. Unless you want to play against bots im afraid this title is officially dead and in the ground. The current average player count numbers are 800 people in off peak, and barely over a 1000 peak. It remains to be seen if Relic will continue to support the title given both its critical and financial failure. 

Also fun fact: Relic has noticed the overwhelming amount of criticism of their game and has set their moderator "Gorb" to full damage control mode. Literally any post criticizing the game is getting instantly locked and deleted on both the official and the steam forums. Pretty sad when half the posts on your forum and locked for discontent, also doesn't help the fans opinion of the title or the developers.

[Update July 28th]

Relics recent patch added some elite skins to the game for free (yay!) and did nothing to address the overwhelming criticism of the deplorable balance introduced 2 patches ago. This is nothing new with Relic as they seem to really struggle with balancing their titles.

 The player count has somehow continued to plummet and now sits at around an average of 600 players at peak time daily, which is absolutely brutal. Most of the time you can see more players in older DOW games and indie titles, its would be funny if it weren't so sad.

 The playerbase has dropped to the point where it is actually impossible to find matches as the game seems to still employ a region filter. There was a post on the official forum of someone actually sitting for over 3 hours in match making looking for a game. Again i will reiterate: if you want to get this game, get it for $20 or less because you will be playing with bots 95% of the time.

The developer has stated that due to poor performance this game will no longer be receiving additional expansions or content.

The developer failed to make a game worth playing.

They want to blame the users for this.

Do not buy this game.

What the hell Relic.
The first Dawn of War was a heavily enjoyable game with a new take on strategy and a great grimdark setting, and my introduction into the tabletop Warhammer 40K. Dawn of War 2 focused on the combat mechanics from company of heroes but with a Dawn of War paintjob, but it was fun, especially now since they dropped the Windows Microsoft Store. The trailer for this game had me hyped, i mean who wasn't? It was suppose to take the combat from DOW 2 with the base mechanics of DOW 1. But instead, Relic played us like a fiddle.

For starters, lack of series features. No more cover, no more Sync kills, no more morale, no more building power generators. Space Marine voices sound awful compared to the previous entries. The graphics look too much like Starcraft. Biggest problem with this game is the Elite/Hero units are overpowered, and your standard units, the ones that compose your army, are just fodder. So instead of playing like a RTS, i feel like im playing a MOBA using my elite units as my heroes with their abilities to wipe out armies, and using my army as a shield. Mind you these are not tactics. The battles themselves feel like a tug of war, with the idea of whoever has the biggest CC abilities will win the battle. 

I have never seen a RTS series get butchered this bad since Command and Conquer 4 Tiberian Twilight. In the meantime, this game is due for exterminatus.

Dawn of War III is the classic "cash grab third installment" curse in action, joining the infamous ranks of Sacred 3, Dead Space 3, and countless other franchises that forgot what made them special.

Everything that could go wrong, went wrong. The gameplay got dumbed down into a MOBA-RTS hybrid that pleases nobody. The plot feels like generic Warhammer fanfiction. The campaign forces you through all three races in rotation instead of letting you pick your poison. Characters are cardboard cutouts with zero personality or depth.

Base building? What base building. You get glorified control points and basic unit production. Strategy? Just spam heavy units from any faction and watch them steamroll everything. The cover system that made Dawn of War II tactical and engaging? Butchered beyond recognition.

The game launched with only three races and died so fast that Relic cancelled all DLC within a year. Players abandoned it for the two decade-old Dawn of War from 2004.

This isn't just disappointing from an RTS standpoint - it's a betrayal of both the Warhammer 40K universe and the Dawn of War legacy.

⚠️ Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III — A Disappointing RTS Entry That Lost Its Way

Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III had the potential to continue the legacy of one of the most beloved RTS franchises, but many players feel it fails to live up to its predecessors and suffers from multiple design and technical problems that undermine the experience. While critics gave it mixed‑to‑positive reviews, user sentiment is significantly more negative, reflecting frustrated expectations. 


🧠 1. Fans Felt It Lost What Made the Series Great

One of the most common complaints is that Dawn of War III doesn’t feel like a true successor to the earlier Dawn of War games. Many players felt the blend of RTS and MOBA‑style elements — including powerful hero units and lane‑style objectives — shifted the focus away from traditional large‑scale strategy that defined the first two titles. 


Reddit users often describe the game as feeling like a MOBA with RTS trimmings, rather than a genuine Dawn of War experience, which left long‑time fans disappointed. 


🐞 2. Technical Issues and Bugs Impact Gameplay

Many players report persistent bugs and an unpolished feel, even months after launch. Common issues include clunky UI behavior, difficulty selecting units reliably, and awkward control responses. Some players described the experience as closer to being a beta tester for a game rather than a finished product, citing problems with camera control, group selection, and mission stability. 


User reviews specifically mention that elements such as UI responsiveness and bugs in campaign missions made certain encounters frustrating or required mission restarts. 


🕹️ 3. Gameplay and Campaign Frustrations

Although the campaign exists, many players found it uninspired and often boring compared with previous entries. Some user commentary describes the campaign as boring or uninspired with slow pacing, while the strategic depth players expected was more shallow or inconsistent. 


Additionally, the resource acquisition and army management in some missions has been criticized as slow, making the core loop feel more like a chore than engaging strategy. 


🧪 4. Balance and Design Choices That Miss the Mark

The introduction of powerful Elite units and hero‑style mechanics was meant to add flair, but many players argue these elements overshadow standard unit tactics and lead to balance problems. Reddit users reported that hero abilities could decimate armies, making fights feel more like hero showcases than thoughtful strategizing. 


Players also took issue with limited faction variety at launch and the sense that key aspects of Warhammer 40K and traditional RTS gameplay were diluted rather than expanded. 


📉 5. Community Backlash and Mixed User Reviews

The Steam user rating for Dawn of War III is significantly lower than its critic score, with many players giving negative feedback due to the issues above. Community sentiment tends to emphasize disappointment relative to Dawn of War I and II, with many advising to revisit the older games instead of this one. 


Many comment threads on fan forums and Reddit reflect that the RTS fanbase felt Dawn of War III missed the strategic essence of earlier games and didn’t justify a full‑price purchase for many. 


🏁 Final Verdict — Disappointment for Long‑Time Fans

Warhammer 40,000: Dawn of War III has some engaging moments and new ideas, but for many players it feels like a step back from what made the franchise great. The design choices, technical issues, and departure from classic RTS mechanics combine to make this entry less satisfying than its predecessors:

✔ Attempts to innovate with hero units and pacing
✘ Moves too far toward MOBA‑style gameplay
✘ Technical bugs and UI frustrations
✘ Campaign pacing issues and uninspired missions
✘ Balance problems and oversimplified systems
✘ Significant community disappointment and mixed user reviews

Overall: ⭐ 5 / 10 — A title that tries to rethink the Dawn of War formula but ends up feeling unfinished and less strategic, disappointing many veteran fans.

The fact they're all but giving it away at $8.00 puts me in a somewhat precarious position. 

If you buy DoW III today, you'll find a community all but dead due to a lack of dev support and a general disillusionment with a game who's mulitplayer isn't exactly 'moba style', but has all the stink of one (Lanes, Towers, and Shield Generators that prevent base ganking before a certain point). While I'm one of the defenders of the brighter art style (I think a lot of hyperfans mistake 'muddiness' with 'grit'), there's absolutely a loss of the slowness and visceral feel that the earlier games had due to smaller unit health pools and much larger units. The fights are way bigger but the feel a lot less impactful. 

So people aren't really playing, is what I'm saying. 

So that leaves the Single Player Campaign, and I have to level with you: Dawn of War III probably has the worst single-player campaign I've ever been put through. It's not just muddy, it's clearly half-finished and half-thought out. A bizzare mix of Isometric Hero Sections (which were terrible in DoW II and they're terrible here) and really under-developed actual RTS fighting. 

It boggles the mind that the game that people remember most fondly, DoW Dark Crusade, was just a RISK board and a bunch of multiplayer maps that [i] still [/i] managed to feel grander and more important than anything Relic has made since despite an absolutely absurd ammount of money and effort. No where is that mistake felt more deeply than in Dawn of War III, where despite being designed more like Dawn of War I, feels like a shallow copy that missed the point. 

So despite the fact they're handing you the game for a pittance, for nothing, I can't recomend it because there's nothing to recommend. The Multi is dead and the Single Player is bad and unless you really want a 3d Model Viewer for Warhammer figures, you're better off with nearly any other game in the series.

I played and loved DoW 1 and 2 for different reasons. DoW 1 was an excellent 40k themed classic ground RTS: big armies, giant waves of doods, tanks and faction exclusive units smashing into each other, what isn't to love? Despite the differences between them, I also had a real love for DoW 2. A hybrid RTS-RPG with loot, an interesting campaign composition and the ability to play through the entire campaign in co op. It traded large scale army smashing in for moment to moment tactics and positioning, Diablo and 40k had a beautiful baby and I was oh so there for it. 

So naturally, when the news broke that Relic was at long last making another one I was pumped. Was, is the keyword in that sentence. 

Dear God-Emperor I wanted to like this, I really did. The critics sure seemed to, and that discrepency between user and critic reviews is what made me try it out. Turns out the people were right. 

SO WHAT'S WRONG WITH IT ANYWAY: Long story short, mixing two great things doesn't always result in Resee's peanutbutter cups if you know what I mean. The issue is that they did both things half way. Basebuilding and support units are back, but they're nowhere near as customizeable or useful as they were in DOW 1. There also are far fewer support units per faction. Every important element from DoW 1 feels like it was distilled and drained of all depth and charm so what we get is Diet DoW. 

As for what they brought in from 2, hoooo boy is that another porblem. Hero units, cool. There's no loot to collect, no customizing their equipment, just whatever they start with and they're practically bulletproof unless they're fighting another hero. It feels like this element was developed without consulting the team working on the smaller units and base building at all. I can take Chapter Master Angelos (that was a nice little touch though) on a solo run through enemy territory, wipe out three control points worth of orks and still have 2/3rds of his health left. 

Didn't try multiplayer but I have heard it's pretty dead, and it brings up an interesting point. Some people have speculated that this game was designed primarily for multiplayer and meant to cater to the E-Sports crowd. I have nothing to back this up, but from my experience that would fit with the end result. A classic example of putting the cart before the horse. Thank the Emperor for steam refunds.

Relic, I'm not mad, I'm just disappointed. I only scold you out of love, and I hope you come back for more 40k.  

tl;dr: Babies first MOBA + Babies first RTS crudely smushed together like playdoh does not a compelling game make. Save your money, go buy the other games or their expansions if you don't already have them.

Dawn of War
I love the Warhammer Universe.  Dawn of War 1 was my first introduction into the franchise.  After watching the first cinematic for DOW1, I grew a beard and became a man.  That intro cinematic perfectly captured the feel of the game.  Dawn of War 1, the expansions, and eventual mods, became the new defacto standard for what I desired in RTS gaming.  Company of Heroes 1 took many of these concepts and improved upon them. Combining the fantastic base building, resource point capture, and squad combat of DOW1 with the new cover system, created what I believe is the finest RTS of its type ever made - Company of Heroes 1.  Also, I had some of the most memorable multiplayer experiences of my life playing DOW1 in 8 player skirmish!
- So EPIC

Twilight
When Dawn of War 2 was announced, I was beyond excited.  When I saw the new graphics engine and heard they were adding the cover system from Company of Heroes, I blacked out in the emperor's light.......or something.  But, DOW2 was not the natural progression of the RTS I came to love and expect.  DOW2 is not a bad game.  The single player had some really interesting aspects, but it was far too linear and limiting.  The skirmish and multiplayer was........non-existent.  I mean, they had those options, but they were nothing compared to the grand RTS battles available in COH1 and DOW1.  I don't know about anyone else, but I just kept replaying the single player campaigns and never touched the skirmish or multiplayer options as they felt so wrong.  DOW2 should have been made bigger, grander, HUGER even.   Instead, we ended up fighting battles with like 4 squads and a single tank.  Super lame and not Warhammery enough for me.  
-Not EPIC

Dusk
Dawn of War 3 had perhaps one of the the greatest intro cinematics of all time, of ALL TIME.  When the announcement trailer released, I watched it 5 times in a row.  The voice-over, detailing the Emperor's love to the peasants, the brutally beautiful imagery of greenskins pulling the arms off terran marines, I mean starship troopers, I mean filthy huummiieess!!  Anyways, the hype was real, I ordered the game as soon as my monitor would accept the cash I was throwing at it.  Then I played the Beta.................This is fun.......I think........but this doesn't feel right.......wait........this is a trick........this isn't Dawn of War........this is something else......Enter the MOBA.  So, as best I can see, someone in Relic/SEGA/Other, was like, "yo, MOBAs and competitive gaming are so hot right now, let's totes do that too!"  The thing is, apparently that same person did no research into what makes MOBAs or competitive games fun and unique.  More than that, they did not ask what makes a MOBA or competitive game successful.  Dozens have come and gone, 1 or 2 have ever succeeded and lasted.  Instead of asking if they could, they didn't ask if they should.  I am not an expert, but I have played enough to know that you don't just go up again Blizzard and Valve, like it's simple to suddenly become a global competitive tournament gaming platform.  DOW1, DOW2, COH1, and COH2 were not made successful because they were competitive.  What made those games hugely popular does not exist in DOW3.  Even DOW2, while very flawed, still had it.  DOW3 has no soul.  Paper thin art direction, cannon fodder space marine units, linear maps, moba defense turrets, point based hero purchases, no cover mechanics (don't get me started on the shield condoms) and micro transactions in abundance, do not an EPIC Warhammer Dawn of War RTS make.
-I lost my faith in the future of Dawn of War.  I fear the producers of the franchise have fallen to Nurgle's influence.  It should all be nuked from orbit, just to be sure....



Dear Developer,

To reclaim the hearts and minds of the Imperium, my recommendations are as follows.  You have already done the right thing by providing updates, patches, and balance changes to DOW 3 since release.  While I do respect and commend you for this effort, I am afraid we are still looking at too little too late.  You are in for an uphill battle now.  

Mod Support - You have provided some mod support, but what this game needs is something like the “Ultimate Apocalypse Mod” created for DOW1.  Allow content creators to take the work you have created and polish it into something greater.  Give the community the tools to create new units, heroes, buildings, re-spec existing units, and adjust economic and gameplay mechanics.  If the framework of DOW3 is expanded upon, it could still have a future.

Unfortunately, a lot of what the fans do not like about DOW3 is gameplay related.  I do not know how much work and effort it would take or if it can even realistically change at this point.  I will try to breakdown the gameplay mechanic changes that I see as needing an overhaul.

Hero Balance - The hero units are interesting and not entirely bad, but the way they are implemented means the gameplay revolves far too much around them.  Hero units are so powerful, the highest level Titan-type heroes can easily decimate armies on their own.  Furthermore, the only true defence against a hero is another hero.  Match outcome seems to be heavily determined by the use of Heroes rather than armies.

Army Balance - In DOW3, armies are expendable, short-lived, swarms, with very little strategic or tactical purpose other than their size.  Size almost always wins out over an attempt to micromanage individual squads and units.  I suggest re-balancing armies with more options (light, medium, heavy armor and weapons), and individual customization (weapons loadouts and upgrades).  In addition, I believe adding experience points for combat to individual squads which unlocks additional abilities and upgrades to improve them over time would help add value to your units.  I also suggest that you look closer at your source material for your implementation. The best I can say for this game is simple:  It looks like Warhammer 40k.  I like that, so it’s a good point.  But is it a “Dawn of War” game?  No, it’s not.  It’s just another RTS.  It departs from the legacy of Dawn of War and returns to the way twitch-gaming.  Is there something to like about it?  Sure, there is… but there’s NOTHING to like about it in way of what I would expect from the Dawn of War series. 

DoW1 was more combat-focused than Starcraft, which was why I loved it... but I greatly favored DoW2, because it emphasized tactical play, which I prefer.  My review centers around this idea.

Most of what made Dawn of War great is not present here. No unit XP/Veterancy. There’s no destructible terrain… there’s almost no cover system, let alone the dynamic and rich cover system of DoW2.  Unit and insignia customization is worse in every way, except for the selection of colors.  Custom, Player-made insignias/banners have been intentionally disallowed.  There's no mixed wargear among squads. The point ticker system has been scrapped, and replaced with a MOBA-like kill objective on a single building.  This disourages tactical play and the relevance of holding territory, while encouraging cannon-fodder play.  Unit preservation, while helpful, is not nearly as emphasized as it should be.  Space Marines are significantly weaker than they should ever be in WH40k lore, because of an over-emphasis on elite units, with all else being “cannon-fodder”.  The extreme fragility of all non-elite units (including vehicles), the lack of a dynamic cover and damage system, and the sheer simplicity and irrelevance of so many gameplay-related design points, spits in the face of tactical play.  

Most (if not all) possibilities for "friendly fire damage" have been removed.  You can literally drop an orbital strike on yourself and your allies and take no damage.  The same goes for every other AoE possibility in the entire game, that I personally remember as of today.  This "feature" is not worthy of any "tactical" game of merit.

The models and animations for the elite units are amazing, with clearly a lot of effort put into it.  In contrast, the models and animations for the common units leave much more to be desired... even seeming cartoonish and cheesy compared to DoW2.  With such an emphasis placed on elite units, and the sheer size of them, the field of view feels too "zoomed out" in order to accommodate viewing the huge elites... while infantry feel like tiny insignificant specs on the battlefield.  This removes the sense of in-your-face grit that should epitomize Warhammer.

The music, the sound effects, the voices, are mostly inferior in feel to those from DoW2, in the sense that they don’t invoke the same feeling of inspiration and glory.  One exception is the Ork voices.  The Orks have more character, voice-wise in this game.  But that's about it.  Space Marine character was definitely degraded across the board.  The amazing graphics of DoW3 don’t make up for the lack of character of the underlying quirks and gameplay dynamics.

For the record:  Some of the pre-release marketing hype about DoW3 was true.  The selection of colors available in the army-painter is impressive.  It's one of the few true improvements here.  It's too bad the rest of the army painter is worse. :)  It increased your maximum army size to something in between DoW1&2.  Yet I disagree with this decision because it encourages a "cannon-fodder" play dynamic.  They created more boxed-in and claustrophobic maps than either of the two previous games.  Instead of having a large sprawling field of territory to explore, hold, and battle for... you have a tiny, fake-feeling e-sports arena to play on.

Do I still Like DoW3 despite all this?  Yes, and no.  I like it because it’s not Starcraft, and because I like Warhammer.  I don’t like it because it's a debacle to everything that the Dawn of War series stood for.  Do I still play it?  Yes… but not because it’s a Dawn of War game… it isn’t.  It’s not Starcraft… that’s basically the summary of why I still play it.  But, in truth, go back to Dawn of War 2, or Company of Heroes 1, if you want a decent tactical game.

For those interested in the REAL reason why Relic titles have gone down the tubes, please read the following history of Relic:

Relic was founded in 1997.  Their first releases (Homeworld and Impossible Creatures), from 1999 and 2003, were reasonable successes.  These were published under Sierra Entertainment.  This was Relic’s “Pre-DawnOfWar” Era.  

In early 2004, publisher THQ acquired Relic.  It was under this publisher that Relic built its most popular, successful, & genre-defining RTS games… notably Dawn of War 1, Company of Heroes 1, and Dawn of War 2… all of which offered a well-designed and refreshing reprieve for gamers who were unsatisfied with typical “Warcraft, Starcraft, CommandNconquer” type of RTS games.  While fans of StarCraft and its ilk were invited to play, Relic did not cater to this crowd… but rather forged a different path, catering to an entirely different model of gameplay and rigidly refusing to water-down its games with twitchy gameplay mechanics.

This departation from the “twitchy and hyper” model of RTS gameplay is what defined the new “Real Time Tactical” genre that set apart Relic’s games from the twitchier RTS games of the past… and stood as a sanctuary in an otherwise chaotic landscape of twitch-gaming debauchery against intelligent gameplay.

After these three smash success titles, publisher THQ found itself struggling financially, and faced with bankruptcy.  Though I’m unfamiliar with the reasons for this financial struggle, I could postulate that intelligent gameplay simply isn’t as popular as twitch gameplay, and thus not as lucrative, despite the loyal and almost cult-following that Relic had by more methodical and tactically-minded gamers.

January 2013 revealed that THQ had dealt with its financial problems by selling Relic to Sega for $26Million USD.  THIS is the marker in time, when Relic games, as fans had come to know and love them, began to go down in the annals of disappointment and mediocrity.

During this time of bankruptcy and selling out to Sega, many of the original Relic development team members had left Relic for new jobs elsewhere.  New “young bucks” were brought in by Sega to replace missing members of the gimped Relic development team.  This "new" Relic team, under direction from Sega to take a development approach of “lucrative” titles, (meaning twitch-style e-sports, as opposed to fan-demanded tactical simulations) is what ultimately caused the debacles of blasphemy that were Company of Heroes 2, and Dawn of War 3.  

Unfortunately, with the original Relic team scattered to the four winds, and Sega pulling all the strings, the days of the glory of Relic are likely gone forever.  The Relic we knew and loved lives on only in name, while Sega and the new Relic crew work only to tarnish its legacy.

After Sega bought Relic from THQ, they even updated the starting splash-screen of Dawn of War 2 (4 years after its release), to clearly display “SEGA”… despite that Sega, and the new Relic team had little to no involvement in its development.  This was very deceptive to “new” players who first discovered Dawn of War 2 after THQ sold Relic to Sega.  It tricked people (without words) into believing that Sega would make a new game comparable to the legacy of Dawn of War 1 and 2… which clearly has been totally disproven by now.

As of the release of Dawn of War 3, Sega and the new Relic team have completely lost my future loyalty to the legacy of Relic titles.  I knew that DoW3 was likely to be a similar debacle to CoH2 and I simply didn’t want to believe it.  I probably will continue riding the DoW3 horse for a few years, if only for sake of nostalgia… but I will think twice, or even three times before I ever trust another Sega or Relic release ever again.

DOW III was always going to struggle with hype. The third child in a wildly expansive and changing series, DOW III realistically faced two possible options. Recreate DOW II and face the cries of unimaginative, or recreate the series (for a third time) and howls of betrayal.

Relic have gone for the latter. This is not a bad thing. I loved the original DOW, but the closer squad tactics and (fairly thin) loot system stole my heart. DOW III sets it's stall out early as a massive army RTS, so sacrificing some of the customisation and RPG elements is reasonable. Sad, but reasonable. Relic's marketing shot themselves by advertising level-up heroes, which is technically true. But Heroes in DOW III are purely unique powerful units. In DOW II you could choose to make your commander a glow-y sword wielding badass or give him an adorable little blaster with obscure backstory neatly included in the description. In DOW III, you choose between giving your infantry or armoured units a buff. It's very cold, calculating and strategic. If you do not see that being a problem, then perhaps this latest DOW is for you, but it's hard not to be disappointed if you had fondness for DOW II.

I tried my hardest to shrug off these initial views and fling myself into the campaign. After all, the game looks gorgeous. You can see that for yourself in the screenshots, and if that doesn't impress you, well then I don't know what you want. The story is pretty bland. Endless, run and secure this point. Now you have this unit, use their special feature to take THIS point. This is fine so far as tutorial missions go, but this ritual continues on far too long. This is exacerbated by the fact you are forced to skip between the three playable races meaning you don't get follow your favourites and ensuring there are constantly new units for you to get to grips with.

What I could not shake is the lack cover. Another feature ditched from DOW II, the only cover provided are very conspicuous shield domes that give you a flat defensive boost if you're in them. Direction, equipment and abilities don't have an impact. This areas are also very sporadic which means much of the game will be attack moving into fog and trying to micro your abilities when the inevitable skirmish break out. It's seems this has been done to facilitate the larger armies and Giant units. It unfortunately makes your route choices seem less impactful. You strategy is judged by your ability management first and composition and position a distant second and third. This again, might appeal to you, in fact I have a strong inkling who this game was made for.

Looking at the gaming market, the success of the arena mode in DOW II, it seems Relic has made DOW III in order to tap into the competitive gaming scene. As someone with more hours in Dota than I’ve had in woman, the feel of DOW III UI is eerily familiar. The very robust match-making, greater EXP gains in multiplayer and lack of clear customisation of units is all very reminiscent of Starcraft or the like. The focus is the multiplayer, and ‘matches’ are meant to be fast paced mob charges with spammed production queues and mastery of research timings. I can’t blame Relic for this change of focus, E-sports is a natural bread-winner. It’s not for me, however. It seems a shame that the richness of Warhammer 40k lore is being pushed to the side for a competitive experience. The game, without an established/competitive pro scene, seems very sparse and bland.

Ultimately DOW III is middle of the road. A 5 or 6 out of 10 depending on your preferences. Middle of the road for a ‘AAA’ title isn’t good enough. The fact that Relic did not make their intention to make a simpler competitive game is the biggest mistake. Let your audience prepare themselves for your new direction, rather than hoping they’ll stick around for the Orks.

While there are positives which might be what you’re looking for; it was for me, as a series fan, a very sad experience and waste of money.

It's difficult to criticise this game as a huge Dawn of War fan, but.. it's difficult to enjoy.

The game in itself is actually not bad, and I'd not have much of a problem with it if it were not a part of the Dawn of War series. But, because it is, it essentially takes the good parts of both of it's predecessors and ruins them while mixing with elements of the MOBA genre.

The MOBA element is probably the worst part about this game; I honestly have no idea why the devs thought it'd be welcomed by the community in a game like DoW. This part of the game makes it impossible to push your enemy early or in other select situations immediately taking away from playstyles that you may have adopted in previous games such as rushes or relocating your base etc. This doesn't just effect the defence of your base, however, this also effects your units with heroes being the main focus of this game leaving the other units to feel weak and irrelevent for the most part. People wanted the new Dawn of War as a fresh RTS to come on the market as you get very few these days - instead it was a hybrid RTS/MOBA that no one wanted. For myself, I thought a combined playstyle of the first and second game in the series would have worked fine.

Other parts of the game are also lacking such as the campaign where the majority of the missions just feel so linear and slow; not to mention that they don't pose a challenge what so ever - I completed the entire campagin on the hardest difficulty with little to no effort. However, the biggest problem of the single-player actually lies in the AI, which is useless; from what I can tell the AI have very clearly been set to do very specific things, it's almost like they run to a rally point and come in waves with specific types of units over and over again regardless of how you're playing - who would have thought that the original Dawn of War from 2004 could have better AI than a game released in 2017?

However, aside from what I've mentioned above, the remaining parts of the game aren't actually all that bad such as the progression system for heroes, the extensive variation in the Army Painter, and some elements of the online competitive games. It was also welcomed to have the act of building structures put back into the game (after being mostly removed in DoW2), although the variety of buildings feels a little sparse and sometimes feels like it's not needed - you'll always build the same structures in the same order every game.

In terms of factions: I honestly had the most fun playing the Ork race where it truly feels like you have a swarm of units; then mixed with the new and improved WAAAGH towers that give a boost to all your units while playing a GREAT MUSIC TRACK while your units are screaming - i'll admit, it's a good feeling (it's probably the best part of this game). I think the Orks could be the one main redeeming factor, and as a long-time competetive RTS player, they feel the most fleshed out when compared to the other 3 races.

The game overall is OKAY - there's something there but it's just not been done quite right and parts of the game feel lazy or unfinished. I would give this game a positive review if it had not been a long awaited third edition to the DoW series, but... because it is, I just cannot bring myself to do so - it's completely overshadowed by it's predecessors. On top of that the devs have completely abandoned the game meaning no further major updates or DLC, without this there's no helping the game at this point. Don't buy it full price, only buy it if you can get it really cheap.

This release makes me the most bitter toward it because it means the series is dead, a series which was my childhood.

As probably heard by now, and supported by the mixed reviews, this game is known as the worst Dawn of War game and likely killed the franchise. But is it really that bad? Especially having just played Dawn of War 1 and 2 recently and having had a much more enjoyable time with them.

I gave the game a chance, and played through the single player campaign, curious to know the continued story of familiar faces. It was fun at times, and annoying at others. So what went wrong, why wasn't I enjoying myself as much?

The game is some kind of hybrid of the first two games and results in an identity crisis where the game tries to be some kind of MOBA with minimal base building. This means there is a ton of micromanagement which is not really my thing when I play Dawn of War. I love to see heavy bolters and terminator squads melt down armies without mercy. Instead, they're more of a sideshow while the heroes do most of the work and they can be tedious to manage and keep checking their cooldowns. Most annoying, the game seems to be broken. Heroes should level up throughout the campaign, in fact I see them getting experience. Yet 17 missions later they were all still stuck at level 1. This seems to be a recurring problem from browsing the forums. There were times my heroes died rather quickly and I wonder if it was because the missions were scaled for higher level heroes but I was still stuck at one.

Base building - it's pointless really.  There's a handful of structures for each faction and pretty much all produce units except one to provide upgrades. Listening posts are back to place on capture points. Where are turrets and defense structures? Missing.  I pretty much just built one of every building and ignored my base builders after that while continuing to mass produce armies to support the heroes. Base building missions were a mixed bag. Early missions felt as if they dragged on for too long. At lower technology level, the early missions don't really have the fun units yet. They were more of a sideshow for the hero to do all the work. In later levels, units can hold their own better, and devastator marines for example were fun to use but something still felt off due to the weird hybrid system. 

The few missions leading up to the final were actually really fun. You get to control giant super units to mow down enemy lines. Now that felt more like warhammer and I no longer felt like slapping enemies with wet noodles. I was having fun finally and eager for the final mission. Annnnnnnnd thumbs down. The final mission made me hate the game. It's pure MOBA nonsense that felt like fighting a MMO boss with infinite adds while you have to kite and scramble around with three characters to avoid the boss's spells. It was the complete opposite of fun, especially the final phase. Eventually it got so bad I was running around with one hero to run out the clock so the others would revive just so I could actually land a hit on the boss. Miserable experience that pissed me off. It totally killed the dawn of war vibe too. Why just three heroes versus the final boss? Going out with a hail of gunfire from supporting armies would have been so much more fun. I had thought I liked the missions without base building more but that last mission really made me miss armies. Having nothing but heroes was not fun and it most certainly wasn't Dawn of War 2 because even Dawn of War 2 knows you should have supporting squad members and seems better balanced.

The game is worth a try for the campaign if you're curious, but only on sale. It's not a terrible game, but the bugs and flawed game style really soured me. If you give it a try, I hope you have a better experience. If you get another bug I encountered - a pop up dialog that won't go away - you can solve it by shutting down the game and restarting it. Or you can do the right thing and just uninstall it.

[h1] Dusk of War [/h1]
War, war never changes. Unless it does. Each time Relic Entertainment approached a new Dawn of War game, they aimed to make “the same game anew”. While the notion is admirable, this credo was obviously increasingly more difficult to follow with each release. On the upside, trying to make the same game from scratch, gave birth to the lovable Space Marine. On the downside, there is also the game in question – Dawn of War III. A title decent enough in itself, just really not a good [i]Dawn of War[/i] game. Without further ado let’s take a close look at the black sheep of the series.

[b] There is only war [/b]
Warhammer 40k: Dawn of War III is the latest instalment in a series of strategy games depicting foremost the story of Blood Ravens Space Marines chapter. After tumultuous events of Dawn of War 2 games, Blood Ravens seem to stand at full strength once more. A returning character of Gabriel Angelos, now a chapter master, leads his battle-brothers to the war for the world of Acheron. A mysterious wandering planet, suddenly appearing from the Warp and allegedly holding a spear of Khaine – an Eldar artefact of untold power. The surface of Acheron soon becomes a site of struggle between Astartes, Eldar and Orcs. Each faction having their own goals revolving around the spear.

The campaign of DoW III explores a direction unseen before in the series. Rather than creating a mini-story for each army or focus exclusively on a single faction, the campaign plays three-fold with all 3 groups swapping after each chapter. It is quite interesting to see the same circumstances portrayed from 3 different perspectives. At times, it also makes for remarkably blunt foreshadowing as you set a trap with one faction to have the other fall right into it in the next chapter. The surprise. Admittedly, this new perspective provides interesting narrative opportunities, although Dawn of War stories of a grand war were never beyond decent. They will sate fans of the genre but are not ground-breaking and were not supposed to be.

Campaign built around three-fold sequence of missions reveals far greater gameplay problems. For the first time in the history of DoW franchise, the game includes only 3 armies – Space Marines, Aeldari and Orcs. An attempt at focusing on 3 factions at once prevents a truly grand campaign present in DoW II, complete with RPG elements, side-missions and character development. Even when covering the single-player mode alone, some of the more severe problems of the game rear its head. First DoW was a “classic” RTS with a clash of grand armies at its core. DoW II shifted that focus in a direction of a more tactical game, where a range of specialist units had to employ their abilities to their full potential. DoW III pushes on even further towards an action angle with introduction of elite units. When the game first released, DoW III was often compared to a MOBA game. Only now do I realise how fitting these descriptions were, as the elite character are at large unstoppable unless met with their counterparts in the opposing force. The armies are nothing but meagre support for the elites until late stages of the game, much like minions or creeps in MOBAs. They are fully capable of determining a victory but are undeniably relegated to the background of the conflict. Several missions in the campaign are focused exclusively on Elites facing against army of ordinary units, highlighting their potential to the point of overblowing it along with the action elements.

Introduction of Elites is also where the greatest crime of DoW III stems from – the oversimplified gameplay, in what technically is a strategy game. Each faction has 10 elites to choose from, with a maximum of 3 pre-selected for each mission. Managing them to a full potential is enough of a hassle on its own. To allow the player to focus on Elites every other aspect of the game has been streamlined to the extreme. Every unit in the game has an counterpart in other factions, reducing the uniqueness of each army. The cover-based environment and buildings are gone, reduced to scarce dome-like structures that can be breached by any melee unit simply walking right in. And the most absurd of all – the stealth covers. They can make any unit invisible until they open fire or the cover itself is entered by an enemy force, no exceptions.

Game play - this is an attempt to combine the traditional base building and larger scaled games of the first game with the moba style heroes and elite units of the second. [h1]Summary[/h1]
It is the dawn of the 41st millennium, and there is only a defunct multiplayer game that combines the worst aspects of RTS with MOBA. This makes me very sad because the campaign was good…really good. But I had to fight the actual game itself to keep liking the single-player campaign. If there is war…there is only war with Relic.
[hr][/hr]
[i]DoW III[/i] does have a handful of good things going for it. It is easily the best 40k story I have encountered in at least 10 years of gaming. The campaign arc was surprisingly compelling. We’ve all been there…you finish a mission, the between mission videos pop, and you say to yourself…wait, I don’t remember that. That never happened in [i]DoW III[/i]. I really was glued to the story. Combine that with extremely faithful writing and great voice acting. I almost want to call the story a 40k masterpiece…almost.

Graphics are great. Gameplay is smooth and free of in game bugs. And well…that’s about where the “good” ends.

Sadly, the game itself is where I have to start with the “bad.” [i]DoW III[/i] went outside the box and tried to sort of combine RTS with MOBA. And much like using Jack Daniels on your Honey Nut Cheerios, you might think it’s worth a try…but you would be terribly, terribly wrong. You have skads of units and options, roughly built on a rock-paper-scissors mechanic (tanks beat infantry, rockets beat tanks, etc.), but the maps make all your units charge down the same path with almost no option to set up strategy or tactics. The worst part…no pause. I don’t know about you, but if I have 12-15 different unit types…each designed with specific uses and counters, there is no way I can give any orders that are more effective than [b]”Leroy Jenkins!!!!”[/b] Once you’re in the thick of it…maybe you will have enough time to get your lascannons to focus the enemy tank.

Ok, so if this is a MOBA, then your champion units should be forces of nature that shake the field of battle. That’s true…for one of your champions. The faction leader does have phenomenal cosmic power, but the rest of the elites are barely better than a normal squad. Until you hit the titans. Those guys are more-or-less unstoppable.  But you only get them in the last mission for each race, so you never actually get to play around with them. If your champion gets wounded, they can slowly heal, but it takes ~20 minutes to go from 1 HP to full…unless you are near a base. That’s not terrible…if the mission you are on even has a base.

Ok, so if this is an RTS, you should be constantly gathering resources and building units. Your first wave might not break the enemy base, but by the time you are done managing that fight you should almost be done building your second wave. Except, resource gathering is so [i]extremely[/i] slow that rebuilding takes nearly 10 minutes. I guess that would be cool if, you know, have to do the dishes or vacuum the living room.  Cripple the base, do some chores, finish the job. If you make a meathead move and get your army killed…you could escape with a few units and rebuild over the next 15 minutes…or you could wipe on purpose and pick up the autosave and save [i]a lot[/i] of time. Games that use your time…literally you sitting there staring at a screen…as punishment for making a bonehead move should be thrown into a blender and the pieces launched into the sun.

I also really [i]loved[/i] how the game does not tell you how to outfit your army in the pre-mission screen. I was halfway through the campaign before I realized that I could swap between elite units. I guess that wasn’t a huge loss since most are trash anyway. But the doctrines were what pissed me off. On the right-hand side of the pre-mission screen, you can select small army-wide buffs…like I want heavy bolters to be extra cool. C’mon guys, you can’t even be bothered to explain how your friggin’ game works in a tutorial?

So…gameplay is bug free…but the rest of the game is riddled with bugs. Oh lord, where to begin… If I unlocked a new skin in a previous play, the game freezes. Saved games frequently disappear from your list if you lose a mission. Oh, and my absolute [i]favorite[/i]…your elite units don’t level in campaign. You watch their XP bar go up at mission end…but then next mission they start right back at 1 again. So, the campaign is just gonna keep getting harder because your elite units are just putzing around at level 1.

Clearly this game was designed for multiplayer. Which is sad, because the campaign is actually really good…but the game itself makes playing the campaign suck.

What makes this double super sadface? Multiplayer is dead…and Relic still wants $40 for this game.  $40 for this unsupported multiplayer game?  The single-player campaign is good, but it’s pretty short (~15 h). Really not worth $40. Maybe $10…maybe.

Brothers and Sisters of the Emperor's Holy Inquisition, I present before you my assessment of Dawn of War III, a title that sought to stand shoulder-to-shoulder with its venerable predecessors, Dawn of War I and II. While the effort of those who labored on this project is acknowledged with due respect, it is my duty to deliver a fair judgment.

Dawn of War III embarked on a noble quest, seeking to blend the grand-scale warfare of Dawn of War I with the tactical, squad-focused intensity of Dawn of War II. However, in its attempt to reconcile these two revered paths, the game has faltered in its execution. The result is a hybrid that does not fully capture the essence of either forebear, leaving the experience somewhat lacking in depth and resonance.

Where Dawn of War I stood as a bastion of strategic conquest, with its base-building and resource management, and where Dawn of War II shone with the brilliance of its focused, character-driven combat, Dawn of War III struggles to achieve the same mastery. The gameplay, while visually impressive and mechanically competent, often feels repetitive—lacking the tactical gravitas and variety that marked the campaigns of old. The cycle of battle—kill, be killed, respawn, repeat—does not inspire the same sense of purpose or glory that once drove us to victory in the Emperor's name.

The narrative, too, while ambitious in scope, fails to ignite the sacred fire within. The story lacks the compelling urgency and emotional weight that once propelled us through the epic sagas of previous titles. It is not that the tale is without merit, but rather that it does not reach the lofty heights set by its predecessors.

In conclusion, Dawn of War III is a title crafted with care, but one that ultimately struggles to stand among the giants that came before it. It is with a heavy heart that I deliver this judgment, for the effort of the creators is not in question. Yet, as Inquisitors of the Emperor, we must measure all things against the highest standards. We hope that future endeavors may learn from these lessons, refining and perfecting the art of war that has long been the hallmark of this venerable series.

In the name of the Emperor, may this judgment serve as both critique and encouragement for those who seek to create worthy offerings in the future.

I've given this more than enough of a chance, and I still can't recommend it. Fans will tell you that there's plenty of options available, and a massive variety between the races, but there really isn't, especially if you've played a lot of RTS games - 

Mechanically, they've basically taken the doctrine system from Company of Heroes 2, but rather than letting you choose between 3 sets of 5 abilities mid game to suit the situation, you're locked into it a choice of 3 before the battle even begins. This essentially limits your strategy entirely - if you pick buildable turrets for example, you best spam them to hell out of them or you may as well have picked another ability. And if your opponent happens to have picked something to increase his anti vehicle / building damage, well, you're already on the back foot before you've even got into the match.

There is very little room to outwit each other mid game due to the most crucial choices being made before the game begins, then it's about implementing the strategy you've chosen, with little room for change.

Fan boys will say " building armies before the match is like the tabletop game" and while that may be true, but as an RTS it simply limits your choices.

It's not all bad though; you can have some really tough matches, large scale battles are a real visual spectacle, and the soundtrack is top quality, but ultimately, compared to the complex nature of Relic's own Company of Heroes 2, this is hollow in comparison, with little to learn, little to keep you engaged, it's doc system works against itself by making certain units irrelevant, and it has some of the most bland and obviously symmetrical map design you'll ever see, 

If you want a better single player RTS game - Get CoH
If you want a better multiplayer RTS game - Get CoH2
If you want a better WH:40k game -  get the original DOW and the Ultimate Apocolypse mod.
